reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as symmetrical, velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of the skin, most often at flexural sites such as the posterior neck, axillae, groin, and inframammary folds
Most commonly a marker of insulin resistance, associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and the metabolic syndrome
Skin tags (acrochordons) frequently accompany the flexural changes
Can be drug-induced (for example by systemic corticosteroids, nicotinic acid, or oestrogens) and forms part of several genetic and endocrine syndromes
Malignant acanthosis nigricans is a paraneoplastic form that is abrupt in onset, extensive, and often involves mucous membranes, the lips, and the palms (tripe palms)
The commonest tumour associated with malignant acanthosis nigricans is gastric, and other gastrointestinal, adenocarcinoma
Circulating insulin acting on keratinocyte and fibroblast growth-factor receptors drives the epidermal proliferation

Management targets the underlying cause: weight reduction and improving insulin sensitivity, stopping a causative drug, or treating an underlying malignancy, with topical retinoids and keratolytics as cosmetic adjuncts
reference.pathophysiology: In most cases circulating insulin, present at high concentrations because of insulin resistance, activates insulin-like growth-factor receptors on keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts, promoting their proliferation and producing the epidermal hyperplasia (papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis) that gives the velvety thickening. In paraneoplastic disease, tumour-derived growth factors such as transforming growth factor-alpha are thought to stimulate the same pathways, which accounts for the abrupt and extensive changes and the mucosal and palmar involvement. Drug-induced and syndromic forms reflect analogous receptor activation through pharmacological or genetic mechanisms.
additionalInvestigations: Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and fasting insulin to assess insulin resistance
Lipid profile and assessment for the metabolic syndrome
Investigation for polycystic ovary syndrome (androgen levels, pelvic ultrasound) in appropriate women
Age-appropriate malignancy screening with gastrointestinal evaluation and endoscopy when malignant acanthosis nigricans is suspected
Review of the drug history for causative agents
Skin biopsy in atypical cases showing hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis
redFlags: Abrupt onset with rapid, extensive spread, especially in a non-obese or older patient, suggesting malignancy
Mucosal, lip, or palmar (tripe palms) involvement pointing to paraneoplastic disease
Associated weight loss, gastrointestinal symptoms, or other constitutional features
Unexplained acanthosis nigricans in a lean patient warranting a search for an endocrinopathy or tumour
reference.prognosis: Benign acanthosis nigricans tends to improve with treatment of insulin resistance or withdrawal of a causative drug; malignant acanthosis nigricans carries the poor prognosis of the associated, often advanced, internal cancer.
pitfalls: Treating the skin cosmetically while overlooking undiagnosed diabetes or the metabolic syndrome
Failing to consider malignancy when the eruption is sudden, extensive, or in an atypical patient
Missing tripe palms and mucosal signs of paraneoplastic disease
Confusing it with confluent and reticulated papillomatosis or pityriasis versicolor
